one_liner: R6RS Scheme compiled to native code at load time; beats LuaJIT, PyPy and Node on integer-heavy interpreter loops, loses badly on boxed-float code.
what_it_does: Chez Scheme is a Scheme implementation whose compiler is part of the runtime: source loaded with `scheme --program` (or entered at the REPL) is compiled on the fly to optimized machine code, and programs can also be precompiled or whole-program compiled to a single binary. It is a language runtime, not a drop-in JIT library: a C host embeds it through the kernel API (Sscheme_init, Sregister_boot_file or Sregister_boot_file_bytes, Sbuild_heap, Scall*), and Scheme calls C through foreign-procedure.
how_it_is_fast: An ahead-of-execution optimizing compiler (nanopass-style passes, cross-library inlining, whole-program optimization) emits native code for x86-64, AArch64, RV64G, LoongArch64 and others; there is no tracing or profiling tier, so code is fast from the first call with no warm-up. optimize-level 3 removes run-time type and bounds checks, and fixnum-specific operators (fx+, fxvector-ref) compile to plain machine instructions; since 10.0.0 the compiler also does type recovery and locally unboxes flonum arithmetic, with flvectors that cooperate with unboxing. A generational garbage collector manages allocation.
when_to_use: Symbolic or integer-heavy workloads (interpreters, tree walking, search with fixnum bit tricks): kostya brainfuck bench.b 1.758 s vs Node.js 2.954 s and LuaJIT 5.686 s; plb2 nqueen 3.54 s vs LuaJIT 5.31 s and PyPy 6.91 s.
You want predictable speed without JIT warm-up: code is compiled when loaded, so short runs do not pay for profiling tiers.

Embedding a garbage-collected scripting language with proper tail calls and first-class continuations into a C host, with modest memory (about 26 MiB RSS for bf.ss vs 244 MiB for Julia and 50 MiB for Node.js in kostya).
Platforms beyond x86-64: native code on AArch64, RV64G, LoongArch64 and PowerPC32, and a portable bytecode (pb) build for anything else, including WebAssembly via Emscripten.
when_not_to_use: Floating-point array code written with generic vectors: plb2 matmul 18.98 s vs LuaJIT 2.66 s, Node 2.88 s and Java 1.14 s, because every element is a boxed flonum; on 10.x rewrite with flvectors and fl operators before judging.
You need a JIT library for your own language or a drop-in replacement for LuaJIT, V8 or PyPy: Chez runs Scheme only, and the compiler is not exposed as a code-generation API for other languages.

You need the speed and cannot accept unsafe mode: both benchmarks run at optimize-level 3, which disables run-time type checks; a type error in that mode is undefined behavior, not an exception. Safe-mode numbers are not published in either suite.
Close races: the mandel.b win over LuaJIT is about 3% (30.884 s vs 31.804 s), and Java beats Chez on both brainfuck tests (1.191 s and 13.041 s).
Heavy string or file I/O: open issues #877 (string operations) and #428 (performance and memory with string and file I/O) report slow paths.

integration.form: executable plus boot files (petite.boot, scheme.boot); the C kernel links into a host as a static library or, on Windows, a DLL or static library
integration.dependencies: C compiler; ncurses (unless --disable-curses) and X11 headers (unless --disable-x11) on Unix; Visual Studio on Windows
integration.min_toolchain: GCC, Clang or similar on Unix; Microsoft Visual Studio 2017, 2019, 2022 or 2026 on Windows; native AArch64, RV64G and LoongArch64 code needs Chez 10.0.0 or later
integration.platforms: Windows x86/x86_64/AArch64; macOS x86/x86_64/AArch64/PowerPC32; Linux x86/x86_64/ARMv6/AArch64/RV64G/LoongArch64/PowerPC32; BSDs, Solaris, Hurd, Haiku, Android, iOS; WebAssembly via the pb bytecode interpreter only
integration.thread_safety: Threaded builds (the default; --nothreads disables them) run native threads; most primitives and simple mutators are thread-safe, but other destructive operations on shared objects need mutexes, code-loading threads' code should run only in that thread or its children, and threads created in C must call Sactivate_thread before touching Scheme data.

gotchas: plb2 harness flaw: its Chez row is version 9.5.8 on an Apple M1, but upstream Chez gained Apple Silicon (AArch64) code generation only with the v9.9.9 merge in Oct 2023 (PR #607) and 10.0.0 lists AArch64 as newly supported, so the 9.5.8 numbers were most likely x86-64 code run under Rosetta 2. plb2 does not say; this biases both nqueen and matmul against Chez.

plb2 matmul.scm stores doubles in a plain vector, so each fl+ and fl* result is heap-allocated; 9.5.8 had no local flonum unboxing or flvectors (both added in 10.0.0), so the 7x loss reflects that version and that code, not Chez 10.x with flvectors.

kostya bf.ss is not tuned: tape-move allocates a new tape record on every > or <, and the tape grows one cell at a time with a full vector copy; Chez still beats Node, LuaJIT and PyPy with it, but cell values are unbounded integers and loops test > 0, the same semantics as the bf.js and bf_jit.lua baselines.

kostya times only the region between the start and stop notifications, so Chez's load-time compilation of bf.ss is excluded while LuaJIT, V8 and PyPy JIT compilation happens inside the timed region; for 1.7 s to 41 s runs the effect is small.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose Chez over Julia when you want a far smaller runtime (26 MiB vs 244 MiB RSS in kostya) and no warm-up on symbolic or integer code where both are close (bench.b 1.758 s vs 1.564 s); over .NET RyuJIT or the Dart VM when you want an embeddable Scheme with tail calls and continuations rather than a managed platform. For floating-point kernels pick Julia, Dart or .NET (plb2 matmul 0.76 s, 2.74 s and 1.38 s vs 18.98 s).
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks (Chez Scheme 10.0.0 from Debian, `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program`, Intel Xeon E-2324G, medians with MAD): brainfuck bench.b 1.758 s vs Node.js v26.5.0 2.954 s, LuaJIT 2.1 5.686 s and PyPy 7.3.23 9.398 s; mandel.b 30.884 s vs 31.804 s, 34.692 s and 41.153 s. plb2 (Chez 9.5.8, Apple M1, hyperfine) nqueen 3.54 s beats LuaJIT, PyPy, Node and Java, but matmul 18.98 s is 7.1x slower than LuaJIT.
status_note: Actively maintained by Cisco with community merges (release notes at Version 10.5.0, May 2026; last commit 2026-10-01); Apache-2.0 and portable, so copyable, though the benchmark numbers come from 10.0.0 and 9.5.8.
